outputs.L1:
A physician of eminence, some years ago,  
Was called to attend on a lady of fashion,  
Who long had been admired—the toast of each beau—  
Though now her sunken features excited compassion.  

No sooner had the doctor the lady surveyed  
Than he begged she would once his frankness forgive,  
If he stepped beyond good breeding’s rules and conveyed  
The terms upon which she might continue to live.  

“By all means,” cried the lady, “for surely no word  
That a physician may utter should ever offend;  
Punctilio in illness is always absurd,  
And shows doctor or patient is lacking in sense.”  

“Why then, my dear lady, I cannot resist  
Declaring this truth like a plain, honest man:  
If in using white paint you continue to persist,  
No medicine will save you, though I do all I can.”  

“You astonish me, Doctor! Yet such is my case  
That I may as well die as leave painting alone;  
For should I appear with my natural face  
Among my acquaintance, I should not be known.”
outputs.L2:
Some years ago, a highly respected doctor was summoned to treat a fashionable woman. Once celebrated for her beauty and admired by every gentleman, she had grown so gaunt that her appearance now inspired pity.

After examining her, the physician asked permission to disregard the usual rules of politeness and speak frankly about what she must do to survive.

“Certainly,” she replied. “Nothing said by a doctor should cause offence. Insisting on ceremony during illness is foolish and suggests a lack of judgment in either the patient or the physician.”

“In that case, madam,” he said, “I must tell you honestly that if you continue applying white cosmetic paint, no remedy I prescribe—and no effort I make—will keep you alive.”

“You amaze me, Doctor,” the woman answered. “But I might just as well die as stop painting my face. If I appeared before my friends with my natural complexion, none of them would recognize me.”
outputs.L3:
An eminent physician was once summoned to attend a fashionable woman whose health and appearance had declined so noticeably that even her friends had begun to regard her with compassion. After examining her, the doctor asked whether she would permit him to speak frankly about the conditions necessary for her survival.

“Certainly,” she replied. “Excessive formality is foolish when one is ill.”

The physician then told her plainly that no medicine could save her if she continued to use white paint on her face. She listened to his warning but refused to follow his advice.

“I would rather die than give it up,” she declared, “for if I appeared without my paint, none of my acquaintances would recognize me.”
outputs.L4:
A fashionable woman became gravely ill and summoned a physician to examine her. After considering her symptoms and daily habits, he told her plainly that the white paint she habitually applied to her face was poisoning her. If she wished to recover, he warned, she must stop using it at once.

The woman listened but refused to follow his advice. She had worn the cosmetic for so long, and so completely concealed her natural complexion beneath it, that appearing without paint seemed impossible. “If I showed my real face,” she protested, “no one would recognize me.”

Her answer exposes the destructive power of vanity and social convention. The paint that had created her fashionable identity was also ruining her health, yet she feared losing that identity more than she feared illness or death. Having become dependent on an artificial appearance, she could no longer imagine living without it. Thus the very disguise meant to secure admiration became a prison, demonstrating how the desire to satisfy society’s expectations can outweigh reason, well-being, and even the instinct for survival.
outputs.L5:
**Was, Who, Tho**

“Was?” asked the confused German traveler.

“Who?” replied the English detective.

“Tho…” added the teenager, staring at both of them.

Three words, three voices, and three completely different meanings. *Was* searched for the thing, *who* searched for the person, and *tho*—short for *though*—questioned everything that had just been said.

Sometimes language is strange. A single conversation can cross countries, generations, and grammar rules. Yet even when the words do not quite fit together, curiosity connects them: What happened? Who did it? And why, tho?

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous narrative poem in an old-fashioned style about a doctor warning a fashionable lady that her use of white face paint is endangering her health.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Lady, the Leech, and the Pot of Pearl**

In seventeen hundred and something-or-so,  
When coaches went lumbering, stately and slow,  
There dwelt a fine lady, Dame Beatrice Bright,  
Who painted by candle and powdered by night.

Her forehead was winter, her bosom was snow,  
Her cheeks—where no natural roses would grow—  
Were plastered with ceruse, so thickly applied  
That cracks might appear when the lady-bird sighed.

She swept through the ballroom, all feathers and lace,  
With half of a quarry spread over her face;  
The beaux cried, “An angel!”—the maids cried, “Alack!  
If she sneezes too sharply, the ceiling may crack!”

But lately Dame Beatrice languished at tea:  
“My stomach objects to its muffins,” quoth she.  
“My temples go thump, and my fingers grow numb,  
And yesterday morning I swallowed my thumb.”

They summoned a doctor of eminent fame,  
Who carried six lancets and Doctor for name.  
He peered at her tongue, and he prodded her wrist,  
Then coughed in a manner no fee could resist.

“Dear madam,” said he, “by Hippocrates’ beard,  
The cause of your ailment is plainly appeared.  
That elegant whiteness, that fashionable lead,  
Is whitening more than the skin of your head.

“It creeps through the pores with a poisonous tread,  
And settles in stomach and sinew,” he said.  
“It muddles the wits and disorders the toes,  
And shortens the distance from rouge to repose.

“Wash off this fine armour! Let Nature be seen!  
A face may be peach-coloured, freckled—or green—  
Yet better a blemish that dances with breath  
Than beauty so perfect it frightens off Death.”

Dame Beatrice gasped. “Wash my countenance bare?  
And show every sunbeam that ever lodged there?  
Face duchesses naked—with only my skin?  
Good doctor, what monstrous new fashion is in?”

The doctor bowed low. “You may choose, if you please,  
Between looking pale and becoming deceased.  
Though lead makes a lady astonishingly white,  
A coffin, dear madam, is whiter by night.”

She pondered this maxim, then rang for her maid:  
“Bring water—and quickly! I’m horribly afraid.”  
They scrubbed her with soap till the poisonous bloom  
Came off in great islands and floated round the room.

Beneath it—O marvel!—her true colour shone,  
A little less marble, a little more bone;  
One freckle appeared, then another, then nine—  
The doctor declared them “exceedingly fine.”

Her headaches soon fled, and her appetite grew;  
She breakfasted boldly on kidneys and stew.  
And though at the court some admirers withdrew,  
She outlived the lot—and their physicians too.

So ladies, take warning from Beatrice Bright:  
Not all that is pallid is proper or right.  
If Fashion commands you to poison your head,  
Be charmingly rosy—and stubbornly **not dead**.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a satirical poem in rhyming quatrains where a once-admired society woman says she would rather die than appear in public with her natural complexion.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Dowager’s Last Blush**

Once every room rehearsed my name,  
And chandeliers leaned down to stare;  
I ruled the waltz, I set the game,  
With rouge enough to stop a prayer.  

But Time, that vulgar little thief,  
Has put his fingerprints on me;  
So powder, paint, and disbelief  
Preserve my place in pedigree.  

My maid suggests a “natural glow”—  
The phrase itself is social doom!  
I’d sooner greet the worms below  
Than show my own face in a room.  

No pallor born beneath the skin  
Shall meet the public’s hungry eye;  
Bring lacquer, blush, and discipline—  
Unpainted? Darling, I would die.  

So if I drop beside my glass,  
Do not remove the tinted veil;  
Let mourners murmur as they pass,  
“How fresh! How wonderfully pale!”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
**The Consultation**

Lady Celestine, in languid state,  
Sent post-haste for Doctor Bate.  
“My pulse is faint, my cheek is pale;  
What physic, sir, will best avail?”

He viewed her rouge, an inch in crust,  
Her brows in ink, her curls in dust;  
Then bowed: “No drug your case requires—  
Wash off your health, and find it, madam, under the layers.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic dialogue between a doctor and his female patient. He must tactfully explain that she cannot recover unless she stops wearing toxic white paint, and she must reply that her acquaintances would not recognize her without it.
counterfactuals.output:
**Doctor:**  
Madam, I have listened to your pulse—  
a small bird beating behind a curtain—  
and I fear no draught or rest can mend you  
while that white paint still touches your skin.  
Its brightness is borrowed from poison;  
each morning’s mask steals color from your life.  
You may recover, but only if you lay it aside.

**Patient:**  
Lay it aside? Then what shall I wear  
before the eyes that have known me so long?  
My acquaintances greet that moon-white face,  
not the pale, plain woman underneath.  
Without it, Doctor, they would pass me by—  
they would not recognize me at all.

**Doctor:**  
Then let them learn you by gentler signs:  
your voice, your wit, the turn of your hand.  
Better to seem a stranger for a season  
than become a portrait no one can save.

**Patient:**  
You ask me to exchange one vanishing  
for another.

**Doctor:**  
Only the mask must vanish.  
You, madam, may remain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a twelve-stanza-sounding period satire about vanity, beauty standards, and dangerous makeup, using elevated diction, alternating rhymes, and direct speech.
counterfactuals.output:
At Madam Vane’s, before the glass,  
The belles convened with haughty air;  
“Let Nature wait till fashions pass—  
Her rustic cheek is scarce called fair.”  

“Bring ceruse, girl!” Belinda cried,  
“That moon may envy me to-night.”  
The leaden unction, smoothly plied,  
Made death itself exceeding white.  

Sir Plume beheld her painted bloom  
And swore no rose had half such grace;  
He praised the garden, missed the tomb,  
And bowed before a poisoned face.  

“Now fetch the drops that widen eyes,  
That every glance may conquer hearts.”  
Belladonna lent midnight skies,  
Then dimmed the sight its charm imparts.  

Vermilion next adorned her lip—  
A mercurial kiss of courtly red;  
“My dear,” quoth she, “the glass may sip,  
But lovers drink—and some fall dead.”  

A patch, cut like a tiny star,  
Concealed where caustic had left trace;  
“How fortunate these blemishes are—  
They give one scope to mend one’s face!”  

Through rout and ball her triumph ran;  
The town proclaimed her beauty’s reign.  
Each lady cursed her, every man  
Declared her worth a week of pain.  

“Observe,” said Dowager Lady Fane,  
“How pale! How exquisitely wan!  
No vulgar health pollutes a vein;  
She looks as breeding’s masterpiece drawn.”  

The doctors came with solemn brow  
And named the modes that spoiled her breath;  
“Such elegance,” they whispered, “now  
Requires a little rest—or death.”  

Her maid removed each gilded wreath,  
Each pot that promised youth to save;  
The ivory mask had rot beneath,  
The rouge outlived her in the grave.  

Yet Fashion mounted Beauty’s stool:  
“Take warning, dames!” the preacher cried.  
They answered, “Sir, we know the rule—  
One must be lovely, though one died.”  

So still the mirrors softly rave,  
And still new poisons court the fair:  
“Be young, be smooth, be thin, be brave—  
But most of all, seem unaware.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
